# Risks and safeguards for rolling out an AI SQL and dashboard tool

The central problem is that you're multiplying production by about 24x (three days to three hours) while review capacity stays fixed at two people. Most of the risks below follow from that.

## What could go wrong

**1. Review becomes the bottleneck, then a rubber stamp.**
Two seniors can't read 25 people's AI-accelerated output. You'll see one of two outcomes. Either the queue grows and the speed gain disappears, or reviewers skim and approve. The second is worse, because the process still looks safe while it no longer is.

**2. Errors get harder to see.**
AI-written SQL rarely fails loudly. It runs and returns a plausible number. Typical failures are join fan-out that double-counts, the wrong definition of "active customer," missing filters, time-zone or fiscal-calendar mismatches, and nulls handled silently. Juniors who didn't write the query are less likely to notice. Polished dashboards also look more authoritative than they deserve to.

**3. Your senior pipeline dries up.**
Seniors are made by years of writing bad SQL and getting corrected. If juniors only prompt and paste, in 18–24 months you'll have people who can't judge the output. You'll also have no one ready to replace the two seniors, who are your single point of failure and are likely to burn out or leave under the review load.

**4. Metric sprawl and conflicting numbers.**
Each plain-English request can yield a slightly different definition of revenue, churn, or conversion. Executives will see two dashboards that disagree. The cost of one visible contradiction is trust in the whole analytics function.

**5. Demand growth and dashboard clutter.**
When requests cost hours, the business asks for ten times as many. You'll accumulate unowned, stale, unreviewed dashboards that people still make decisions from.

**6. One bad number reaches an executive decision.**
Eventually something wrong gets through, and the question will be who approved it. With diffuse accountability, the answer will be "the AI" or "the seniors who couldn't review it all."

**7. Data access and privacy.**
Plain-English access to everything can pull sensitive columns (HR, customer PII, pricing) into drafts and exports by people who shouldn't see them. Check what data leaves your environment as well.

**8. The pilot may have flattered you.**
It measured turnaround, not accuracy. Pilots typically involve motivated people, simpler requests, and heavier senior attention than you can sustain at 25 users.

## What to put in place before rollout

**Fix the definitions first.**
- Build a governed semantic layer or certified metrics catalog, with one definition each for revenue, churn, active user, and so on. Point the tool at it so it composes from vetted metrics instead of inventing them.
- Restrict the tool's data access to approved tables and columns, using role-based permissions.

**Replace "seniors review everything" with tiered review.**
- Tier 1 (exploratory, internal, self-serve): no senior review. Label it "unreviewed draft."
- Tier 2 (team-level decisions): peer review by a trained junior using a checklist.
- Tier 3 (executive, financial, external, or regulatory): mandatory senior review, with a hard rule that nothing reaches executives without a reviewer's name on it.
- Sample Tier 1 and 2 output each week to measure the real error rate.

**Make output checkable.**
- Require the tool to show the SQL, the assumptions it made, the filters applied, and row counts alongside every result.
- Add automated checks, such as totals reconciled to known source-of-truth figures, duplicate-key and null checks, and a regression suite of questions with known answers that you re-run whenever the model or schema changes.
- Make the requester state the expected rough answer before running. If the result is off by 2x, that's a flag.

**Protect skill development.**
- Keep juniors writing and explaining SQL by hand on a regular basis (for example, weekly exercises or one in five tasks done without the tool).
- Require each junior to be able to explain any query they submit. Review them on that, not on volume.
- Define a growth path so some juniors are being trained to be reviewers, and you have a succession plan for the two seniors.

**Redefine the senior role.**
- Make them owners of the metrics layer, test suite, and review standards, plus Tier 3 review. Stop using them as a human QA gate on everything.
- Consider hiring or promoting a third reviewer before rollout, not after the first incident.

**Control sprawl.**
- Give every dashboard an owner and an expiry date, and archive anything unused for 90 days.
- Add a duplicate-detection step: before building, check whether a certified dashboard already answers the question.

**Roll out in stages and measure the right things.**
- Start with 5–8 analysts, then expand.
- Track error rate (from sampling), reviewer queue time, rework rate, number of metric-definition conflicts, executive-facing corrections, and junior skill assessments, not just turnaround.
- Set a pause trigger in advance, such as an error rate above X% in sampled work or any incorrect number reaching executives.

**Assign accountability.**
Write down that the analyst who submits the work owns its correctness, whatever tool produced it.

## If you only do three things

1. Build the certified metrics layer.
2. Move to risk-tiered review, with senior sign-off required for anything executive-facing.
3. Measure accuracy by sampling from day one, because speed will look great regardless.

I can turn this into a rollout checklist or a one-page risk memo for leadership if that would help.
